passages.t: Can you pull in Leviathan with a hook?
passages.happening:
“Can you pull in Leviathan with a hook or tie down his tongue with a rope? Can you put a cord through his nose or pierce his jaw with a hook?” (verses 1-2). Will he beg Job for mercy, or make a covenant to serve him for life? Can Job keep him as a pet bird, on a leash for the girls of his house? Will traders bargain over him? “If you lay a hand on him, you will remember the battle and never repeat it!” (verse 8).

“No one is so fierce as to rouse Leviathan. Then who is able to stand against Me? Who has given to Me that I should repay him? Everything under heaven is Mine” (verses 10-11).
passages.hearers:
God's second speech reaches its height with Leviathan, a creature of the sea that no hook can catch and no weapon can wound.

The opening questions take scenes from everyday life and make them absurd. Fishermen landed fish with hooks and ropes. Captives and slaves were sometimes led by a rope or ring through the nose, as Assyrian carvings show. A covenant could bind a servant to a master for life. Children kept birds, and merchants divided a catch among themselves. Can Leviathan be treated in any of these ways? Plainly not.

Then the point turns. If no one dares to rouse Leviathan, who can stand against the God who made him? And verse 11 states the principle beneath the whole book: no one has a claim on God. Everything under heaven is his.
passages.later: Paul takes up verse 11 near the end of his long argument about God's mercy: ‘Who has first given to God, that God should repay him?’ (Romans 11:35). For Paul it means that no one can put God in their debt, and that everything God gives is grace.
passages.asks: God asked who has ever given to him, that he should repay. Ask whether you have treated God as owing you something. And ask what changes if everything you have is a gift.

passages.t: Scales, fire, and an iron-hard frame
passages.happening:
“I cannot keep silent about his limbs, his power and graceful form” (verse 12). Who can strip off his outer coat or open the doors of his jaws, ringed with teeth? His rows of scales are his pride, so tightly joined that no air can come between them.

‘His snorting flashes with light, and his eyes are like the rays of dawn’ (verse 18). Firebrands stream from his mouth, and sparks fly. Smoke pours from his nostrils as from a boiling pot. ‘His breath sets coals ablaze, and flames pour from his mouth’ (verse 21). Strength is in his neck, and terror dances before him. “His chest is as hard as a rock, as hard as a lower millstone!” (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
Notice how God speaks of this creature: he cannot keep silent about its power and its graceful form. The thing Job cannot face is something God delights in.

Many scholars think the portrait draws on the Nile crocodile, whose armored scales, fearsome teeth and resistance to weapons fit much of the description. Crocodiles were familiar in Egypt, where they were feared and even worshiped. The fiery breath and smoking nostrils point beyond any ordinary animal to the dragon of old poetry. A lower millstone was the heavy, fixed stone of a hand mill, the hardest thing a household had.
passages.later: A psalm says that God made this creature for his own delight: “There the ships pass, and Leviathan, which You formed to frolic there” (Psalm 104:26).
passages.asks: God could not keep silent about the beauty of a creature that terrifies people. Ask what in creation frightens you, and whether you can see it as God's work. And ask whether you believe that what you fear most is under his hand.

passages.happening:
‘When Leviathan rises up, the mighty are terrified; they withdraw before his thrashing’ (verse 25). Sword, spear, dart and arrow do nothing. He counts iron as straw and bronze as rotten wood. Slingstones are chaff to him, ‘and he laughs at the sound of the lance’ (verse 29).

His underside is like jagged broken pottery, and he leaves a track in the mud. ‘He makes the depths seethe like a cauldron; he makes the sea like a jar of ointment’ (verse 31). “He leaves a glistening wake behind him; one would think the deep had white hair!” (verse 32).

Nothing on earth is his equal, a creature without fear. ‘He looks down on all the haughty; he is king over all the proud’ (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
The description moves from head to tail and ends with the wake through the sea, churned to foam like ointment boiling in a pot, white like an old man's hair.

The last line is the verdict: Leviathan is king over all the proud. It links back to 40:11-12, where God challenged Job to humble every proud man. Job cannot master even this creature. God made it, and God rules it.

The word for the deep in verse 31, tehom, is the word for the waters in Genesis 1:2.
passages.later: Elsewhere Leviathan is the many-headed monster God defeats: “You crushed the heads of Leviathan; You fed him to the creatures of the desert” (Psalm 74:14).
passages.hard:
Is Leviathan a real animal like the crocodile, or a mythical monster?

Readers have argued for both. Those who favor a real animal point out that the whole speech so far has described real creatures, from lions and ravens to the war horse and Behemoth, and that the crocodile fits the scales, teeth and resistance to weapons remarkably well. They read the fiery breath as poetic exaggeration. Those who favor a mythic creature point to the other Old Testament passages where Leviathan is a many-headed sea serpent (Psalm 74:14; Isaiah 27:1), and to the older poems from Ugarit about a serpent called Litan, and they argue that no ordinary animal breathes fire.

Many scholars take a middle path. The poet describes an animal like the crocodile in the language of the chaos dragon, so that one creature stands for everything in the world that humans fear and cannot master. These notes take no side.

Whatever Leviathan is, the chapter's point is the same. It is a creature. God made it, and God delights in it. The thing Job cannot face is under God's hand.
passages.asks: Leviathan is king over the proud, and God is king over Leviathan. Ask what pride in you needs to meet something greater than itself. And ask where you have tried to stand against God rather than with him.
